26: ## Early Christian witnesses to the substitution

The Qur’an says that those who claimed to have killed the Messiah did not kill him and did not crucify him, “but it was made to appear so to them” (4:157). Three Christian texts from within two centuries of the crucifixion say the same, and two of them name the man who carried the cross. They are set here at the point in the story where the gospels have Simon of Cyrene pressed into service, each read against the Qur’an as the measure, with what is kept and what is set aside stated in its note.

The Gospel of Basilides is lost. Basilides taught in Alexandria in the first half of the second century, and nothing he wrote survives; what he taught about the crucifixion is known only from Irenaeus of Lyons, who reported it around 180 CE in order to condemn it.

- [agree] Basilides, on the crucifixion. When they led him out to crucify him, Simon of Cyrene was pressed to carry the cross; and Simon was changed into the likeness of Jesus, and Jesus into the likeness of Simon, so that they crucified Simon in ignorance and error, supposing him to be Jesus; and Jesus himself was not crucified, but departed to Him who had sent him.{{fn:Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.24.4, in paraphrase; for Simon of Cyrene see Mark 15:21, Matthew 27:32 and Luke 23:26. Agrees with Qur’an 4:157, “they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them”, and with the reading of the classical commentators, several of whom named Simon of Cyrene as the one made to resemble him. Irenaeus adds that Jesus stood by and laughed at those who thought they held him. That detail belongs to the Gnostic contempt for the body and for those bound to it; it has no place in the Qur’anic portrait of a messenger of mercy, and it is set aside. Irenaeus is a hostile witness, and whether Basilides’ account stood in a gospel book of his own or was a tradition he handed on is not known: see Bart D. Ehrman, “The Lost Gospel of Basilides”, The Bart Ehrman Blog, 1 July 2023.}}
### The Second Treatise of the Great Seth

A Coptic text of the third century, copied in the fourth and found at Nag Hammadi in 1945, in which the risen Christ speaks in the first person. Most of it is Gnostic teaching that the Qur’an rejects, and the note says so. One passage records the same tradition as Basilides, and it is given here in the website’s own words.

- [agree] The Second Treatise of the Great Seth, on the crucifixion. They devised their plan against me, but I did not succumb to it as they intended, and I was not afflicted. I did not die in reality but in appearance. It was another who drank the gall and the vinegar; it was not I. It was another whom they struck with the reed; it was another, Simon, who bore the cross on his shoulder; it was another on whom they set the crown of thorns. They nailed their own man to their death, and they did not see me, for they were deaf and blind.{{fn:Nag Hammadi Codex VII, 2, 55-56, in the website’s own words after the translation of Roger A. Bullard and Joseph A. Gibbons in The Nag Hammadi Library in English, ed. James M. Robinson, 3rd ed. (Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1988). The passage agrees with Qur’an 4:157 on the one point for which it is used: that the crucifixion was made to appear otherwise to those who carried it out, and that another was taken for him. Everything around that point is set aside, and the reader should know what. The speaker says he was laughing at their ignorance, which the Qur’an’s messenger of mercy does not do. He denies that he had a real body at all, where the Qur’an says that he and his mother ate food (5:75). And the treatise calls Adam, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, Solomon, Moses and the prophets “laughingstocks” and derides the God who says “I am God and there is no other beside me” as an ignorant lesser power, where the Qur’an honours every one of those prophets and makes that very sentence its first truth (2:163; 47:19). As a whole the work conflicts with the Qur’an and is not a source for this gospel. It is kept here as a witness, not as a teaching: evidence that some Christians, within two centuries of the event, held that the one on the cross was not he.}}

A Coptic text of the third century from the same Nag Hammadi codex as the Second Treatise, in which Peter is shown the crucifixion and asks what he is seeing. It is a Gnostic work throughout, and the note says what is set aside. Its answer to Peter’s question is given here in the website’s own words.

- [agree] The Apocalypse of Peter, on the crucifixion. I saw him seemingly seized by them, and I said, “What do I see, Lord? Is it you yourself they take? Or who is this one on the tree, and is it another whose hands and feet they strike?” The Saviour said to me, “The one into whose hands and feet they drive the nails is the substitute, one who came into being in his likeness. The living one stands near him, whom they seized and released. See how they do not know what they are doing: they have put to shame the son of their own glory in place of my servant.”{{fn:Nag Hammadi Codex VII, 3, 81-82, in the website’s own words after the translation of James Brashler and Roger A. Bullard in The Nag Hammadi Library in English, ed. James M. Robinson, 3rd ed. (Leiden: E. J. Brill, 1988). The passage agrees with Qur’an 4:157 on the one point for which it is used: that the one nailed to the cross was another, made in his likeness, and that those who did it did not know. Set aside, and said so: the text has the living Jesus “glad and laughing on the tree” and laughing again at their lack of perception, which the Qur’an’s messenger of mercy does not do; it explains the substitute as his “fleshly part” and the living one as an “incorporeal body” and “intellectual Spirit”, a docetism the Qur’an rejects, since he and his mother ate food (5:75); and it divides humanity into immortal souls and souls made for destruction, and calls those who “name themselves bishop and deacons” dry canals, which is its quarrel with the Great Church and no concern of the measure. As a whole the work conflicts with the Qur’an and is not a source for this gospel. It is kept here as a witness, not as a teaching.}}

These are the oldest Christian records of the belief the Qur’an states, older than any surviving Muslim commentary by five centuries. What the Qur’an affirms, that the matter was made to appear otherwise to them, some Christians had taught from the beginning; what those Christians built around it, a Christ without a real body who held the cross in contempt, the Qur’an rejects as firmly as the church did. See the end of his earthly mission.
